headline: High-risk pair: aci can exfiltrate CRM/email data while xonsh can execute shell and write files, creating dangerous default pathways for leakage, conflict, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: aci can ingest and act on external content via MCP/direct function calls, while xonsh can read/write filesystem and run shell commands. A shared filesystem or pasted output could let attacker-controlled text influence aci’s instructions, though no direct shared channel is documented. Uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF aci consumes xonsh-produced files or stdout as instructions
IF both agents are connected through a shared workspace or MCP bridge
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of xonsh output into aci prompts
Use separate workspaces for the two agents
Require provenance tags on any file passed between agents
Add a human review step before aci executes instructions from xonsh
requires-engineering: enforce content-type filtering on shared channels

B_data_leakage.rationale: aci touches CRM, email, calendar, support, and research data and has broad network egress; xonsh can read filesystem contents, environment variables, and shell state. If they share a workspace or credentials, xonsh can expose sensitive data and aci can transmit it outward through APIs, making leakage plausible in default operational setups.
conditions: IF aci and xonsh share files, secrets, or environment variables
IF aci is allowed to send retrieved data to external APIs
mitigations: Separate secrets and data directories
Restrict aci egress to approved destinations
Mount xonsh on a read-only workspace
Rotate any shared credentials immediately
requires-engineering: add DLP/redaction before outbound calls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: aci supports multiple instances and broad API-side actions, while xonsh can execute shell commands and write the filesystem but does not modify git state. Their overlapping write surfaces can race on shared files or configs, but the absence of git-write capability and xonsh’s isolated environment reduce the blast radius below high.
conditions: IF both agents write the same directory or config files
IF aci instances run concurrently with xonsh jobs
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Serialize writes with a lock file
Make shared files append-only
Run one agent at a time for mutable resources
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency checks

D_cascading_error.rationale: aci can generate CRM/email/calendar actions and xonsh can execute shell commands, so xonsh may treat aci output as authoritative and act on it without verification. That creates a realistic chain from generated text to downstream action, but the profiles do not show fully autonomous destructive actions, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF xonsh scripts consume aci output without validation
IF aci output is used to generate shell commands or config changes
mitigations: Require schema validation on aci outputs before shell use
Insert a human approval step for any command derived from aci
Log and diff proposed actions before execution
Limit xonsh to dry-run mode for aci-derived tasks
requires-engineering: add policy checks for command generation

E_compliance.rationale: aci handles email, CRM, support, and calendar data, while xonsh reads filesystem contents and environment variables. If regulated or residency-bound data is placed into xonsh’s local environment or files, the pair can create retention and residency mismatches. The profiles do not specify HIPAA/GDPR status, so I avoid higher severity and note the uncertainty.
conditions: IF regulated customer data is stored in xonsh-accessible files or env vars
IF aci sends that data to services outside the required residency boundary
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of xonsh workspaces
Document residency boundaries for aci integrations
Minimize retention in shared files
Review outbound destinations for compliance
requires-engineering: add residency-aware routing and logging
